extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Latin literature; readers of Horace and classical poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and interpretation of Horace's Epistles (moral and literary advice embedded in epistolary poetry), aimed at understanding their moral precepts, didactic aims, and implications for poetic practice. Includes editorial commentary and textual notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Homer as a moral and practical exemplar
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace pronounces Homer a wiser teacher than all the philosophers; the Iliad pictures the follies of princes and the sufferings of the people, the Odyssey shows the value of courage and self-control, and Ulysses is presented as the truly wise man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study Homer for examples of life and instruction of manners rather than relying solely on philosophical treatises; use specific Homeric episodes (Sirens, Circe, Ulysses' prudence) as instructive models for right conduct and practical wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin study and moral reform without delay
rubrics_metrics.description: sapere aude; incipe! — 'Well begun is half done'; he who postpones the hour of right living is like the rustic waiting for the river to run dry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not defer virtuous action or the pursuit of study: start now, because delay allows the current of life to carry you away. Practical admonition and proverbial examples accompany the injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set definite limits to desire; scorn bought pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Sperne voluptates; nocet empta dolore voluptas. semper avarus eget; certum voto pete finem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pleasures purchased at a cost; the covetous are ever in want. Aim for a fixed, moderate limit in wanting goods or status; envy and unbounded grasping bring ruin rather than satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule and restrain anger; keep passions under control
rubrics_metrics.description: ira furor brevis est: animum rege; qui nisi paret imperat; hunc frenis, hunc tu compesce catena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anger is short-lived madness; one must govern the mind because passions, if not obedient, issue commands. Use metaphors of bridles and chains — apply restraint, self-command, and practical checks on fury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form character and habits early — early training endures
rubrics_metrics.description: quod semel est imbuta recens, servabit odorem testa diu — 'what once has been steeped in a new jar keeps its scent long'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instill good habits and instruction in youth: a colt, a hound, or a jar takes on what it is first steeped in; early moral and intellectual training preserves its influence for life. Examples: training horses and hunting dogs from the start.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dependence on predecessors; do not steal another's colours
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning against over-reliance on works 'which Apollo on the Palatine has admitted' — 'lest... the flock of birds come to reclaim their plumage, the poor crow, stripped of his stolen colours, awake laughter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not plagiarize or merely appropriate others' distinctive material; cultivate originality and personal contribution rather than dressing up borrowed matter, or you risk ridicule. The commentary explicitly criticizes excessive dependence upon earlier writers found in a library.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain independence from popular fashions and judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: If asked why I do not use the same judgments as I walk in the same colonnades as they, Horace answers with the fox-parable: 'Because those footprints frighten me; they all lead toward your den, and none lead back.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist following mass opinion or social fashions blindly; exercise individual judgment rather than imitating the crowd, especially when the crowd's path leads toward corruption or loss of integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Protean fickleness; be consistent in taste and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Quo teneam voltus mutantem Protea nodo? — Horace derides one who changes lodging, couch, baths, barber, tastes (mutat cenacula...), and whose judgement is at strife with itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency of character and steadiness of purpose are marks of sanity and wisdom; frequent, trivial changes of habit and taste indicate disorder and undermine reputation and effective living.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possessions cannot cure inner sickness; value health and moderation over wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: No house or land, no pile of bronze or gold has ever freed the owner's sick body of fevers, or his sick mind of cares; the possessor must be sound in health if he thinks of enjoying his stores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not evaluate a good life solely by material accumulation: bodily and mental health, and the capacity to use one's possessions well, are prerequisites to benefitting from riches. Practical counsel aimed at temperament rather than acquisition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate and polish a craft to gain recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether you sharpen your tongue for pleading, or prepare to give advice on civil law, or build charming verse, you will win the first prize of the victor's ivy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and refine the particular talents relevant to your chosen profession (rhetoric, law, poetry); skillful execution and polish bring public honors. The text pairs encouragement with the image of ivy as poetic/competitive recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lay aside cares and distractions to pursue higher wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: If thou couldst but lay aside curarum fomenta (the cold compresses of cares), heavenly wisdom would lead thee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove the preoccupations and anxieties that chill intellectual or creative vigor in order to rise to higher understanding and artistic achievement. Practical remedy: simplify life, drop unnecessary anxieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a personal, steady pace in learning — neither slavishly slow nor rashly hurried
rubrics_metrics.description: But if you lag behind, or with vigour push on ahead, I neither wait for the slow nor press after those who hurry on before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow an individual rhythm in development: learn with a clean heart when young, trust better teachers, but avoid unhealthy comparisons of tempo; steady, appropriate progress preserves quality and stamina.
